summary: EcoCell Earth Intelligence is a free web map and 3D globe that turns more than 20 years of NASA Earth observations into clear answers: what changed, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. Users pick one of 10 NASA variables (methane from Aqua AIRS, rainfall from GPM, vegetation, land temperature and evapotranspiration from MODIS, water storage from GRACE/GRACE-FO, soil moisture and air temperature from FLDAS, ocean temperature and chlorophyll from Aqua MODIS). They then click the world, a continent, a country or a single 1° block. For each zone, the site shows the trend with a 95% confidence interval and a significance test (Sen slope, Mann-Kendall with autocorrelation correction, false discovery rate control). It also shows when the change happened, how it compares with the world, and which other variables changed in the same place. The data update automatically every night. A voice assistant, Eco, guides users in English and Portuguese. This matters because NASA data are open but hard to read: EcoCell lets students, communities and decision makers detect real Earth system trends in a few clicks, with honest uncertainty.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

EcoCell Earth Intelligence is a free web map and 3D globe that answers four questions about our planet: what changes, where, how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. It uses only NASA open data: 10 variables from missions and models. These are methane (Aqua AIRS), rainfall (GPM IMERG), vegetation, land surface temperature and evapotranspiration (Terra MODIS), total water storage (GRACE/GRACE-FO), soil moisture and air temperature (FLDAS), and sea surface temperature and ocean chlorophyll (Aqua MODIS).

HOW IT WORKS

1. Choose a variable: users pick one of the 10 NASA variables on a 2D map or a 3D globe with NASA Blue Marble imagery.

2. Click a zone: the world, a continent, a country, or a single 1° block (about 110 km).

3. Read the answer: the "When did it change?" panel shows:

- the trend with a 95% confidence interval;

- whether it is significant (Sen slope, Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation, and false discovery rate control across all blocks, q < 0.05);

- the trend in three periods (2002-2008, 2009-2018, 2019-today), in 5-year moving windows, and its acceleration;

- how the zone compares with the world;

- which other variables changed in the same place.

4. Explore more: rankings show which countries and variables change most, any variable can be animated year by year, and data can be exported as CSV.

5. Ask Eco: an animated voice assistant gives a guided tour in English and Portuguese. Users say "Hey Eco" to run map commands instantly ("zoom to Brazil", "show rainfall", "switch to 3D") or to ask open questions. Answers come from an AI model that receives only the site's current NASA results and is instructed not to invent numbers.

6. Automatic updates: a GitHub Actions workflow downloads new NASA data every night, recomputes all trends and rebuilds the site.

Example result: global methane measured by AIRS rises +5.6 ppb per year since 2002 (95% CI +4.9 to +6.2). The rise is accelerating (+0.18 ppb/yr each year, CI +0.04 to +0.32), with the fastest growth around 2021 (about +11.6 ppb/yr in 5-year windows).

BENEFITS

- Turns more than 20 years of NASA observations into clear answers that students, teachers, journalists, communities and local decision makers can understand in a few clicks, with no coding or GIS skills.

- Every number carries its uncertainty, so users can tell a real trend from noise.

- It is free, open source, works on phones and offline after the first visit, and is available in English and Portuguese.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want people, especially in regions with few local monitoring stations such as Angola and much of Africa, to see where and when their environment changed: water, vegetation, rainfall, heat and methane. They can then decide where to monitor or act first.

As an application example, the site connects methane trends to EcoCell, our methane-capture concept: methane-eating bacteria in a microbial fuel cell produce electricity, which is used to make hydrogen and then ammonia. An animated digital twin explains how it works. The concept has not yet been validated in the lab, and the site states this clearly.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Data processing: Python (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Shapely, earthengine-api, earthaccess), with NASA Earthdata (AIRS) and Google Earth Engine (NASA collections).

- Website: JavaScript, D3.js, WebGL, HTML and CSS, hosted on GitHub Pages.

- Automation: GitHub Actions, for the daily update.

- Voice: the Web Speech API (speech recognition and synthesis) and a Cloudflare Worker connected to Google Gemini for open questions.

- No special hardware: everything runs in a web browser.

CREATIVITY

- Detective approach: instead of only showing pretty maps, EcoCell tests every block for significance and tells users when a change happened, not just that it happened.

- Same answer at every scale: users get the same kind of answer for the world, a continent, a country or a single block, and the site compares each zone with the global trend.

- Natural interaction: a voice assistant lets people explore NASA data by speaking in their own language.

- From data to action: the methane results link to a possible solution (EcoCell) and to a digital twin that simulates it.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: confidence intervals, autocorrelation correction and false discovery rate control avoid false alarms. Regional differences that a second instrument did not confirm are labelled as indicative. Known limits are stated: AIRS measures methane in the mid troposphere (about 400 hPa), not at the surface, and the most recent windows are less certain.

- Only NASA data: as the challenge asks, all variables come from NASA missions and models. GPM is a joint mission with JAXA, and GRACE and GRACE-FO are joint missions with the German agencies DLR and GFZ.

- Accessibility: plain language, two languages, voice control, a phone-friendly layout, and colours chosen for colour-blind users.

- Performance: the page loads quickly and the 3D globe draws on the GPU, so it works on modest phones and slow connections.

- Sustainability: the daily automatic update means the site keeps working with new NASA data without manual effort.

- Privacy and security: the AI key is stored only on the server, never on the site.
dataRefs: AIRS/Aqua L3 Monthly Standard Physical Retrieval V7.0 (AIRS3STM) – methane
GPM IMERG Final Precipitation L3 Monthly V07 (GPM_3IMERGM) – rainfall
MODIS/Terra Land Surface Temperature 8-Day L3 V061 (MOD11A2)
MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day L3 V061 (MOD13A2) – NDVI
MODIS/Terra Net Evapotranspiration Gap-Filled 8-Day L4 V061 (MOD16A2GF)
GRACE and GRACE-FO JPL Global Mascons RL06.3 v04 – total water storage
FLDAS Noah Land Surface Model L4 Global Monthly (FLDAS_NOAH01_C_GL_M) – soil moisture and air temperature
MODIS Aqua Level-3 Ocean Color and SST (NASA OB.DAAC) – sea surface temperature and chlorophyll
NASA Blue Marble: Next Generation – base imagery
NASA Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS) – map tiles
projectRefs: JAXA - GPM mission partner (GPM IMERG rainfall)
GFZ Potsdam - GRACE-FO mission partner (water storage)
Google Earth Engine - access to NASA data collections
GitHub Actions - daily automatic data update
Cloudflare Workers - secure server for the Eco assistant
Google Gemini API - AI answers of the Eco assistant
Claude (Anthropic) - AI coding and writing assistant
Web Speech API - voice recognition and speech
IPCC AR6 WG1 - methane global warming potential (GWP100 = 29.8)
Hamed and Rao (1998) - Mann-Kendall autocorrelation correction
Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) - false discovery rate
